name: Aisha Dubois

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hi Aisha, thanks for doing this. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no links to tech companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you tell me is confidential, so you can give me your public line and your private one. Can you start by telling me what a normal working day looks like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm site lead for a crew that puts up timber-frame apartment blocks, four and five storeys. The walls and floors come from a factory as big panels, we call them cassettes, and my job is getting them off the truck, onto the crane and fixed in the right place in the right order. My day starts at six with the delivery schedule on my phone, and by seven I've usually rearranged it twice because a truck is stuck on the ring road.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what wears you down?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I enjoy the puzzle. I use an AI assistant every day to rework the crane sequence when something's late, and to translate the safety briefing for the guys who speak Romanian and Portuguese, and when that all clicks we can close in a whole floor in two days. What wears me down is people above me who think it's still 1995, and the cold. Mostly the cold, if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hype, huh. I'd be a bit disappointed, to be honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, fair enough, it was a useful tool and not much more. I'd keep using what works and stop reading the big predictions. Online I'd probably post something about how it still saves me an hour a day, even if it didn't change the world.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be a little sad, because I'd been excited about what robots could do for the heavy, dangerous parts of the job. Nobody should be wrecking their back lifting plasterboard for 40 years. But for me personally it's fine, I'm good at what I do and I'd keep moving up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on like now, using AI for scheduling and translation, and keep pushing my company to try new kit. I'd probably take a site management course in the next year, since I'm already doing most of that job. My savings would just keep growing, I've got about a year put aside plus some index funds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, with a bit of 'oh well'. Like a gig getting cancelled that you only half wanted to go to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the plasterboard. Is there someone specific you were thinking of?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My uncle Karim. He's a dryliner, he puts up the inside walls and ceilings, and at 50 he can't lift his arms above his head without wincing. I got into the trade partly because of him. I was kind of hoping robots would arrive in time to save the next Karim.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would anything at your company change in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much. The office would keep their fancy software and I'd keep fighting them to let me use mine. There's a project manager, Henrik, who still prints every email. In the plateau world, Henrik wins, and I have to listen to him say I told you so.

S0.say: Fair enough, AI was a useful tool and not much more. She'd keep using what works, ignore the big predictions, and post that it still saves her an hour a day.
S0.think: She'd be a little sad that robots won't take over the heavy, dangerous lifting that wrecks workers' bodies. For her own career, she's confident she'd keep moving up.
S0.do: Keeps using AI for scheduling and translation and pushes her company to try new equipment. Takes a site management course within the year while her savings and index funds keep growing.
S0.feel: Calm with a touch of disappointment, like a cancelled gig she only half wanted to attend.
S0.quote: I was kind of hoping robots would arrive in time to save the next Karim.
S0.fieldNote: Aisha is the rare worker who is disappointed by the calm scenario. Her interest in technology is tied to protecting bodies like her uncle's, which links her adaptability to her progressive values. Her money position is clearly comfortable and she knows it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. That's the one I'd bet on. It's already starting on my site.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a big chance, if we do it fairly. Robots should take the dangerous lifting, and the workers who get moved should be retrained on the company's money, not their own. I'd say that loudly in the union and online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think this is good for me. I'm the one on site who already uses these tools, so I'd become the person who runs the new kit. The bit that keeps me honest is knowing that people like Karim and some of my crew could get squeezed if nobody fights for them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Straight away, I'd ask my company to make me the lead on trialling any new kit, like the robotic total station that marks out the floor or the exoskeletons for lifting. I'd probably buy my own drone for site surveys, around a thousand, and learn to use it properly in my own time. I'd also push the union to get a tech agreement signed before the big rollouts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit excited even. It feels like the thing I've been waiting for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd become the person who runs the new kit. What happens to the people on your crew who don't want to learn it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the hard part. Ion, one of my fixers, is brilliant with his hands but he barely uses his phone. I'd want to teach him myself, slowly, in Romanian if I have to, with the translation app on. If the company tried to just swap him for a machine, I'd make a lot of noise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you see any downside for yourself at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe I'd end up behind a screen more and on the deck less. I didn't get into construction to sit in a cabin. I'd want to keep at least half my day out there with the panels and the wind.

S1.say: This is a big chance if done fairly: robots take dangerous lifting and moved workers get retrained on the company's money. She'd say it loudly in the union and online.
S1.think: It's good for her, since she already uses the tools and would run the new equipment. She worries that coworkers less comfortable with technology could be squeezed without someone fighting for them.
S1.do: Asks to lead trials of robotic layout tools and exoskeletons, and buys a drone for about a thousand to learn surveys. Pushes the union for a technology agreement before big rollouts.
S1.feel: Calm and a bit excited, as if this is what she's been waiting for.
S1.quote: I'd want to teach him myself, slowly, in Romanian if I have to, with the translation app on.
S1.fieldNote: Aisha combines early adoption with a strong sense of duty to her crew, and the two pull in the same direction here. Her only personal worry is losing time outdoors. She'd spend her own money on equipment, which fits her comfort with risk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Wow. Okay, that's fast even for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In public I'd say this is too fast for society, even if the technology is amazing. We'd need emergency rules: income support, limits on layoffs, and a say for workers in how robots get rolled out. I'd be at the protests, but carrying a sign that says share it, not stop it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd land on my feet, at least at first, because someone has to coordinate the robots and I already do that kind of thinking. But if AGI can do almost any work, then eventually it can coordinate too, so my edge might only last a year or two. And Jonas tests software for a living, which is probably the first thing to go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First thing, I'd offer my company a plan for how to bring in robot crews safely on our sites, with me running it, before they hire some outside firm to do it. I'd sign up for any robot operation training going, even unpaid. I'd also push the union to demand that robot productivity gets shared, like a cut of the savings going into a fund for workers who lose hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd be excited and scared in the same breath, and I'd probably not sleep much for a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Jonas's job is probably first to go. Have the two of you ever talked about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little, half joking. He says when the robots come, I'll be the breadwinner and he'll learn to cook properly. We've got enough saved that neither of us would starve. But I don't think he'd be as relaxed as he pretends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You described your edge lasting a year or two. What then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I don't know. Maybe I'd go into teaching people how to work alongside the machines, or into politics at the local level. I'd want to be one of the people deciding how the gains get shared, because if I'm not in that room, someone from a tech company will be.

S2.say: This is too fast for society, even if the technology is impressive, so emergency rules on income, layoffs and worker input are needed. She'd protest under a 'share it, not stop it' sign.
S2.think: She'd land on her feet at first by coordinating robots, but that edge may last only a year or two. Her partner Jonas tests software, which she expects to go first.
S2.do: Offers her company a plan to bring robot crews onto their sites with her in charge, and takes any robot operation training, even unpaid. Pushes the union to demand a share of robot savings for workers who lose hours.
S2.feel: Anxious, excited and scared at once, with a sleepless month.
S2.quote: I'd be at the protests, but carrying a sign that says share it, not stop it.
S2.fieldNote: Even the fastest scenario doesn't make Aisha reject the technology, but she sees clearly that her own advantage is temporary. Her money takes the edge off. Her instinct is to get into the room where decisions are made, which is a mix of ambition and politics.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's a much better runway. I can work with that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, good, we've got time to get this right, so let's start now. Every trade college should be teaching robot supervision next year, and unions should be negotiating the rollout terms today. I'd say it in every meeting I'm in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years is my sweet spot. I could get properly qualified, maybe even start a small firm with a couple of friends that installs and supervises robot crews for builders. It's still scary for the end point, but the middle part sounds like a lot of fun for someone like me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In year one I'd do a part-time course in construction robotics, there's one at the technical college for about two thousand. By year three, I'd probably put fifteen or twenty thousand of my savings into a worker co-op with two friends from the trade, offering robot setup and site coordination. I'd keep doing my union stuff on the side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly because of what comes after. The five years themselves, I'd actually enjoy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: A co-op rather than a regular company. Why that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I don't want to be the boss who replaces everyone with robots and keeps the profit. If the three of us own it equally and we bring people from our crews in as members, then the gains stay with people who built houses. That's the whole point for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your uncle Karim in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him to come in with us. He knows how a wall goes together better than any engineer, and robots still need someone to tell them when something looks wrong. He'd grumble, but he'd be good at it.

S3.say: With time to get it right, trade colleges should teach robot supervision now and unions should negotiate rollout terms today. She'd say it in every meeting.
S3.think: Five years is her sweet spot to qualify and start a small firm that installs and supervises robot crews. The end point still scares her, but she'd enjoy the years before it.
S3.do: Takes a two-thousand construction robotics course in year one, then by year three puts fifteen to twenty thousand into a worker co-op with two friends. Keeps up her union work alongside.
S3.feel: Uneasy about what comes after, but she'd enjoy the five years themselves.
S3.quote: If the three of us own it equally and we bring people from our crews in as members, then the gains stay with people who built houses.
S3.fieldNote: Her business idea is shaped by her values: a co-op, not a standard firm, so the gains stay with workers. Five years turns AGI from a threat into a project for her. Inviting her uncle in shows how she ties her plans back to family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be 37, which is a good age to have built something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's no excuse for leaving anyone behind with ten years' notice. Free retraining, a share of the gains for workers, and decent income for people who can't switch. I'd probably be campaigning for that at a local level.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd be fine, more than fine probably. I'd have time to grow the co-op idea slowly, and to make sure my crew and people like Ion have a real path. What would bother me is the bigger question of what people do with themselves when work isn't the centre of life anymore.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my current job for the first few years and learn everything I can about the robot systems as they arrive on other sites. I'd start teaching evening classes at the college on digital tools for tradespeople, which would pay a bit and build a network. Around year five I'd launch the co-op, and I'd keep putting money into index funds the whole time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. Excited about the decade, a little wistful about what the trade turns into.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said work might not be the centre of life. What would that mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm not sure. Building is a big part of who I am, I like being the woman who can read a drawing faster than the engineer. If that skill stops mattering, I'd probably still build things for fun, like furniture, or help friends fix up their places for free. I'd find a way to stay useful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a moment in that decade you're dreading?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The day the last human crew on our company's books gets stood down. I'd want to be there and buy everyone a meal. It sounds dramatic, but you'd want to mark it somehow.

S4.say: With ten years' notice, there's no excuse for leaving anyone behind: free retraining, shared gains and decent income for those who can't switch. She'd campaign locally for it.
S4.think: She expects to be more than fine, with time to grow her co-op idea slowly and give her crew a path. What bothers her is what people do with themselves once work isn't central.
S4.do: Keeps her job for a few years while learning the robot systems, and teaches evening classes on digital tools for tradespeople. Launches the co-op around year five and keeps investing in index funds.
S4.feel: Mostly calm and excited, a little wistful about what the trade becomes.
S4.quote: The day the last human crew on our company's books gets stood down. I'd want to be there and buy everyone a meal.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade's warning, Aisha's worries become philosophical rather than financial. She would build income from teaching and the co-op, using her adaptability fully. The dread she names is emotional, a farewell to the crew culture she loves.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Not for me so much, but because there's no time for anyone to adjust, and the people on my crew who are slower with tech would get crushed. What would help is a law that makes companies share robot savings with the workers they replace, and paid retraining starting immediately.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who should own the robots. I think that's the whole question. If the people who build the houses own a piece of the machines that build them, most of my fears go away.

headlineQuote: If the people who build the houses own a piece of the machines that build them, most of my fears go away.
portrait: Aisha Dubois is a 27-year-old site lead on timber-frame apartment builds who uses AI every day for crane schedules and safety translations, and who got into the trade partly because of her uncle's worn-out body. She is calm, even a little disappointed, in the AI Plateau and excited by Steady Disruption, where she'd lead trials of new equipment. The two-year AGI picture makes her anxious, mostly for slower-to-adapt crewmates and her partner Jonas, a software tester. With five or ten years she plans robotics training and a worker co-op so that the gains stay with tradespeople.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because there would be no time to adjust and crewmates who are slower with technology would be crushed.
whatWouldHelp: A law making companies share robot savings with the workers they replace, plus paid retraining that starts immediately.
